A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EVA framework and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. v1 Appendices A–G largely correspond to v2 Appendices B–H; v2 adds experimental, complexity-analysis and disclosure sections.

before.justification: v1 reports original recognition and detection results on DVS128-Gesture, N-Cars and Gen1, together with architecture, pretraining-objective and patch-size ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds N-Caltech101 recognition, shared-backbone Gen1 comparisons, latency measurements and event-downsampling experiments.

M1.justification: Event tokenization, time-difference embedding, RWKV-6 encoding, MVHS outputs, patch-wise processing and MRP/NRP objectives remain unchanged. Renaming learned representations as features and evaluating another downstream backbone do not introduce a new encoder or learning procedure.

E1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds N-Caltech101, extending evaluation to static-image-derived event recognition across 100 object classes plus background. This substantially broadens the represented visual categories and acquisition conditions beyond v1's gesture recognition, car classification and automotive detection. All three original datasets remain.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds DAGr-L to the Gen1 comparison. New Table 10 compares EVA against Voxel, ERGO-12, Pillar, HOTS and TORE under a shared backbone; Table 9 also introduces comparators including E2VID for N-Caltech101. The original DVS128-Gesture and N-Cars comparator sets remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds an identical-Swin-V2 Gen1 comparison with representation-update latency, an N-Caltech101 evaluation following EST's split, context-length timing sweeps and frozen-encoder downsampling tests from 8192 to 512 events. Original experimental settings are retained; chunk lengths move from the main text to Appendix E without changing.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 and Appendix A.3 add latency scaling with context length and robustness to event downsampling, examining the accuracy–throughput tradeoff under processing constraints. The original component, SSL-objective, patch-size, classifier and target-window analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: v2 newly states that experimental random seeds are fixed and introduces latency error bars in Figure 5. It does not specify seed values, repetition counts or what the bars represent. These are reporting additions, not evidence of increased repeated-run evaluation.

E6.justification: Original benchmark and ablation scores remain unchanged, including 47.7% Gen1 mAP. New results include 86.3% N-Caltech101 accuracy, 49.7% EVA-L mAP with Swin V2, and 95.1% gesture FVA under eightfold downsampling. The Swin result uses a different backbone and is not a same-setting improvement. New Table 11 reports ALERT-Tr. (+LMM) FVA as 86.2%, conflicting with the retained 89.2% in Table 1.

T1.justification: New Appendix I gives per-event O(M) and sequence-level O(TM) complexity arguments for EVA and comparative expressions for other representations in Table 15. The existing RWKV/MVHS mathematics, learning objectives and model-size reduction derivations remain substantively unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: an expressive asynchronous encoder, generalizable self-supervised features, improved A2S recognition and the claimed first successful A2S detection framework. Changing 47.7 mAP to 0.477 in the abstract is equivalent scaling, not a stronger result.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantial discussion of Gen1 throughput constraints, patch parallelism, sensor-resolution scaling and downsampling tradeoffs. Appendix F newly interprets feature channels as retaining different temporal histories and defers quantitative analysis of their dynamics. The original limitations concerning actual deployment and restricted model size remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-code access statement, identifies Python/CUDA for timing experiments and supplies a tensor-shape/data-flow diagram in Figure 6. Existing preprocessing and training details are retained, including relocated chunk-loss settings. The explicit sinusoidal embedding formulas in v1 are replaced by a shorter verbal description.

R1.justification: New Section 2.2 positions EVA against token-wise Transformers, event-processing state-space models and concurrent Event2Vec work. The asynchronous-processing review also expands its graph-method coverage and revises its criticisms of graph temporal accumulation and EventNet's lack of hierarchical learning. These are substantive positioning changes beyond citation-format updates.

P1.justification: The introduction and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten, and learned-representation terminology changes to feature terminology throughout. Tokenization and embedding subsections are merged, chunk-loss explanations move to the appendix, and the appendix structure expands alongside reproducibility and LLM-usage statements.

P2.justification: v2 adds six tables, a latency plot and a data-flow diagram, updates diagram labels, relocates Figure 4 and adopts conference headers and formatting. The original visualization becomes Figure 7 with resizing and an expanded caption; its underlying images are unchanged.

improvement.justification: The shared-backbone comparison, broader recognition coverage and downsampling tests strengthen the empirical support for EVA's expressivity and practical tradeoffs, while the code-access statement improves reproducibility information. The gain is limited by sparse settings for new experiments, undefined latency error bars and the conflicting LMM FVA in Tables 1 and 11. Real-world deployment remains untested.
